articles.title: We Love This Listing: A Farmyard Reimagined as a Family Home
articles.deck: In Country Life, garden designer James Alexander-Sinclair recalls the six-bedroom country house he built within a former farmyard—and later sold.
paragraphs: A courtyard as the starting point

Alexander-Sinclair describes finding a concrete courtyard with tumble-down barns beside his parents-in-law’s home. The appeal here is the transformation: an agricultural site became the setting for a family house, with proximity to grandparents helping to shape the decision.
Six bedrooms, one clear footprint

According to his account, the new house was L-shaped, with six bedrooms, all within the original courtyard. That relationship between a substantial house and an existing footprint offers a more particular architectural story than size alone.
Salvage and compromise

He reports dismantling the old structures to reuse their bricks and roof slates, although the gathered slates were stolen. He also recalls economising on radiators after the house exceeded their budget. Those admissions give the project a refreshingly unvarnished character: ambition came with practical trade-offs.
The connection beyond the wall

One detail stands out in his recollection: a gap in the garden wall allowed access to his wife’s parents’ house and the woods. He says the family sold after the children left home. This is a retrospective portrait, not a claim of current availability; its strongest theme is a home shaped around a particular chapter of family life.

A room inside the reservoir

According to Country Life, the former cast-iron tank held 38,000 gallons of water; its converted space now contains the ninth-floor Prospect Room, with windows on every side and 360-degree London views. Making height habitable

Country Life describes a separate new tower containing a lift and bathrooms, connected to the original by glazed walkways. It also reports that the original York stone staircase remains. The glass-and-steel addition known as The Cube houses the main living area, Country Life reports, with kitchen and dining space below a reception room. Our reading is that this provides a useful architectural counterpoint: the tower supplies the vertical drama, while the addition gives everyday rooms a distinct setting.

articles.title: We Love This Listing: Grangewood House opens onto the High Weald
articles.deck: Terraced gardens and a conservatory make the setting part of this historic Fairlight home’s character.
paragraphs: A house with a long outlook

Grangewood House sits just outside Fairlight, where its conservatory looks across the High Weald. Strutt & Parker identifies the property as Grade II listed and describes stone elevations, tall sash windows and a vaulted entrance hall. Those details give the house a strong architectural identity before the garden comes into view.
The landscape unfolds

The agent reports 7.77 acres, with terraces stepping through the gardens toward a fountain, followed by meadow and woodland. A pool and a separate annexe above the garage add further places to spend time. The progression from formal planting to a looser landscape is what catches our attention.
Why we love this listing

Country Life included this East Sussex home in its November 8 selection at £3.1 million. Our favourite feature is the relationship between the rooms and the grounds: the outlook gives the interiors a subject beyond their own period details.

articles.title: We Love This Listing: Le Paradis looks out over Cinnamon Bay
articles.deck: Tile roofs and tropical foliage sit below the horizon at this hillside estate on St. John.
paragraphs: The roofs above the bay

In the auctioneer’s photograph of Le Paradis, the rooftops occupy a surprisingly small part of the scene. Trees climb almost to the eaves, and the bright arc of Cinnamon Bay appears below the house. That is the distinction worth making about this St. John address. It offers a view from above the beach, with enough elevation to see how the shoreline bends around the forest.
A place to pause

Concierge Auctions describes an eight-bedroom residence on an acre, with a palm-lined approach and a saltwater pool. Inside, polished sycamore cabinetry and a kitchen island of tiger’s eye give people at the counter something to look at even with the view behind them. The auctioneer’s November 16 announcement scheduled bidding to open December 8. We would start a tour on the terrace, then walk back into the kitchen to see how the light changes. articles.title: We Love This Listing: A Cowes chapel with a working waterfront past
articles.deck: At Alexandra House, the chapel windows survive and the river runs right past the building.
paragraphs: Between street and harbour

Stand on the street side of Alexandra House and the clues are all there. Three arched upper windows sit beneath a pediment, with a glimpse of blue water down the side of the building. Spence Willard places the property on the sheltered western bank of the Medina. Country Life reported a £1.65 million asking price on November 13.
A project with a history

The building began as a Wesleyan chapel in 1831. Boatbuilder Sam Saunders later used it as a workshop. That sequence makes the deep-water pontoon more than a picturesque extra. Water access once helped explain why people worked here. For a buyer today, the starting point is the shell and the berth. Country Life describes the former planning consent as lapsed, so the proposed glazed accommodation belongs in the drawings until the planning position changes. Want to see your property here?

articles.title: We Love This Listing: Denes House opens from a village street to a valley view
articles.deck: In Burwash, a white Georgian frontage hides a house whose principal rooms turn toward the High Weald.
paragraphs: A short walk from the gate

Denes House meets the High Street through a walled garden and an iron gate. Blue Book describes a fanlight over the entrance and a skylight over the flagstoned hall. That second source of daylight matters. A visitor can step away from the bright front windows and still follow the curve of the staircase by natural light. Country Life pictured the house in its November 20 feature and reported an asking price of £1.75 million.
How the back of the house works

The owners made the old kitchen into a sitting room and built a kitchen and breakfast room at the rear. The drawing room also opens south, through French windows onto a terrace overlooking the garden. Those details give the village house two distinct outlooks. The street is close enough to see from the front gate, while the rooms where people gather look out across the valley. Want to see your property here?

articles.title: We Love This Listing: Creston Manor puts five residences to work on a California ranch
articles.deck: Vineyard, pastures, stables and five homes share nearly 578 acres in San Luis Obispo County.
paragraphs: A ranch read from the air

In the auctioneer’s aerial photograph, Creston Manor looks like a patchwork. Trees trace the edges of fields and a cluster of buildings occupies only a small part of the valley. Looking at it that way explains the appeal of this California property better than counting bedrooms. The vineyard and winery are part of the estate, as are the barns, stables and open pasture.
Several places to stay

Concierge Auctions traces the ranch to 1900 and describes five residences and a separate private suite. A group staying here could spread out across different buildings while sharing the working landscape around them. The November 11 announcement identifies Alex Trebek as a former owner and says bidding was scheduled to open December 4. What we would want to explore first is the distance between the houses and the winery, a detail an aerial view can suggest and a walk can settle. Want to see your property here?

articles.title: We Love This Listing: The Quaives keeps a working garden beside a musician’s retreat
articles.deck: Christine McVie’s former country home near Canterbury has three cottages, a greenhouse and roughly 18 acres of contrasting garden spaces.
paragraphs: Where the garden meets the house

The kitchen at The Quaives has doors into the garden, while the drawing room opens to a south-facing terrace. Those are two quite different ways out of the same house. One suggests crossing the threshold with muddy boots and something just picked. The other suggests pulling up a chair and staying a while. A kitchen garden and a 35-foot greenhouse give that distinction some substance.
Room across the estate

The Spaces reported on November 18 that the Grade II-listed house near Canterbury was offered at £3 million through Harding Green. Christine McVie bought it in 1990 and lived there for 25 years. Seven bedrooms are arranged across three floors in the main house, and the estate includes three cottages. One bears the name Songbird, a quiet connection to the songwriter in a place with a character all its own. Want to see your property here?

articles.title: We Love This Listing: One roof for one Tribeca penthouse
articles.deck: The roof at 427 Washington Street covers the building’s footprint. A former industrial neighbourhood makes an unusually good backdrop for a garden.
paragraphs: The block from above

Look at the listing photograph from above and you can trace the outline of the roof garden against the streets below. This is the private outdoor space for the penthouse at 427 Washington Street. Robb Report puts it at roughly 4,600 square feet. A water tower shares the roof with raised planting beds and places to sit. The neighbouring rooftops give the garden a distinctly New York horizon.
The floor below

Downstairs, the apartment takes a different approach to the same view. Eighteen windows face in four directions. A 48-foot great room accommodates both dining and lounging, and an alcove beside the dining area has room for a grand piano. The two bedrooms are part of the current arrangement. What draws us here is the freedom to step from a long, light-filled loft into a garden of comparable scale without crossing the street. Want to see your property here?

articles.title: We Love This Listing: An indoor pool opens to the lawn on Belvedere Island
articles.deck: On the western slope of Belvedere Island, 337 Belvedere Avenue puts the swimming pool and the lawn on speaking terms.
paragraphs: Two ways to enjoy the view

There are plenty of places to look out across San Francisco Bay at 337 Belvedere Avenue. The one that caught our eye was the swimming pool. Concierge Auctions describes a 60-foot indoor pool that opens to the lawn. A swimmer gets the shelter of a room and can step directly outside afterward. A second kitchen on the recreation level makes it easy to imagine spending an afternoon down there.
A hillside in the evening

The six-bedroom house was built in 2008 on a little more than half an acre. Its terraces face the afternoon and evening light, with views toward the bridge and the city. In the auctioneer’s photograph, the skyline is a narrow silhouette beyond a broad sweep of bay. Concierge Auctions announced on November 12 that bidding was scheduled to open December 4. articles.title: We Love This Listing: A two-storey library at a Danbury estate
articles.deck: The main house at 125 Long Ridge Road brings its bookshelves, bedrooms and family spaces into conversation with the land outside.
paragraphs: The long view

In the listing photograph, a pale house stands at the end of an approach lined with trees. Woodland spreads out behind it, making the extent of this Danbury property easier to picture. Robb Report covered the 80-acre estate on November 19 and reported an asking price of $12.5 million through Cindy Raney of Coldwell Banker Realty.
A room worth lingering in

Inside, the library is the place we would start. Bookshelves line two storeys, giving one quiet activity an unusually generous share of the house. The family room offers a different experience, opening directly to a covered patio. Upstairs, four of the five bedrooms have Juliet balconies, while the principal bedroom has a full private balcony. Those distinctions matter: a door you can open for air serves a different purpose from a place to sit outside with a book. Want to see your property here?

item.title: This London Water Tower Has Been Turned Into a Contemporary $3.7 Million Residence
item.summary: Dating to the 1860s, the original structure has been paired with a glass and steel extension.

illustrationDraft.title: We Love This Listing: A London Water Tower With a New Perspective
illustrationDraft.deck: Victorian brickwork, a glass-and-steel addition and a former water tank turned lookout give this London conversion its distinctive architectural rhythm.
paragraphs: Infrastructure, Reconsidered

According to Robb Report, this tower was built in the 1860s to supply the nearby Lambeth Workhouse and converted into a roughly 4,500-square-foot residence in 2011. Its appeal lies in that dramatic change of purpose: an imposing piece of civic infrastructure rethought at a domestic scale.
A Deliberate Contrast

Robb Report describes Venetian Gothic brickwork paired with an ultramodern glass-and-steel extension called the Cube. Its ground floor contains an open-plan kitchen and dining room alongside a reception room with full-height sliding glass doors. Architecturally, the contrast is more compelling than an attempt to make the addition disappear.
A Home That Climbs

The report identifies an original York stone staircase connecting the floors, plus a separate added elevator tower. Five bedrooms and four bathrooms occupy the tower. That vertical arrangement suggests a different domestic rhythm from a sprawling mansion, with movement between levels central to the design.
The Tank Becomes the Destination

At the top, Robb Report places the Prospect Room inside the original cast-iron water tank, with windows on all four sides and views including the London Eye. This is the conversion’s strongest idea: giving the tower’s defining industrial component a new role rather than treating it as a relic.

item.title: This $13.9 Million Venice Beach Compound Has Ties to Charlie Chaplin
item.summary: The nine-bedroom home once served as a boarding house that attracted the likes of Charlie Chaplin.

illustrationDraft.title: We Love This Listing: A 1911 Venice Beach House With Layers of Character
illustrationDraft.deck: A triple-lot estate near the beach pairs a boarding-house past with timber ceilings, distinctive fireplaces and generous gathering spaces.
paragraphs: A history beyond the headline

According to Robb Report, this Venice Beach property was built in 1911 for Warren Wilson, founder of the Los Angeles Daily Journal. It later became a boarding house whose guests included Charlie Chaplin and Abbot Kinney. Those connections are compelling, but the architectural continuity makes the stronger editorial case.
Character in the materials

Robb Report identifies retained hardwood floors, wood-beam ceilings on both levels, and decorative tile and brick fireplaces. We love the combination: several distinct materials carrying the history, rather than one period detail doing all the work.
Rooms with individual identities

The publication reports nine bedrooms and seven bathrooms, describing a plaid-wallpapered bedroom with a private balcony and another bedroom paired with a navy-blue sitting room. The appeal here is individuality rather than uniformity—a fitting quality for a house with such a layered past.
Shared spaces, inside and out

Robb Report describes a wood-paneled living area with a working wood-burning fireplace, a dining banquette curving into a bay window, and a brick garden walkway connecting a deck and covered porch. To us, these varied gathering spaces are the feature’s quiet counterweight to its famous-name history.

item.title: This $14 Million Equestrian Estate Sits Within a Double-Gated Orange County Community
item.summary: The three-acre spread, located in the exclusive Los Ranchos Estates, features a four-stall barn and riding arena.

illustrationDraft.title: We Love This Listing: A Three-Acre Equestrian Estate in Coto de Caza
illustrationDraft.deck: Horse facilities anchor this Orange County estate, where Robb Report describes a renovated main residence, separate guest house and generous spaces for gathering.
paragraphs: The Horses Come First

According to Robb Report, the three-acre property includes a four-stall barn with a tack room, office and saloon, alongside a riding arena and three pastures. That combination gives the equestrian identity substance: this is not simply a large house borrowing ranch style.
Rustic, Without Being One-Note

Robb Report dates the original construction to 1981 and notes subsequent renovations. Its description of the 8,400-square-foot main residence pairs cathedral ceilings and exposed beams with a neutral palette. The appeal is that balance: substantial architectural gestures, with finishes that sound comparatively restrained.
Room for Different Gatherings

The publication reports dual stone-top kitchen islands, a living-room wet bar and a temperature-controlled wine cellar with approximately 1,700-bottle capacity and a dedicated tasting room. Read together, these suggest several distinct settings for hosting, rather than one oversized entertaining space expected to do everything.
A Separate Place to Stay

Robb Report also describes a one-bedroom guest house with an open-plan living room, dining room and kitchen, plus access to a sauna and steam room. Editorially, that separate accommodation is a compelling counterpoint to the main residence’s scale: room for company without making every gathering communal.

item.title: This Olson Kundig-Designed Home Frames Hawaii’s Rugged Landscape
item.summary: The 6,500-square-foot residence on the Big Island's Kona Coast is made up of a series of glass-walled pavilions set within a courtyard garden.

illustrationDraft.title: We Love This Listing: A Kona Coast Home Composed Around Lava and Courtyards
illustrationDraft.deck: Olson Kundig’s pavilion-style residence pairs ocean-facing outdoor spaces with a remarkably deliberate approach to privacy, shade and volcanic terrain.
paragraphs: A collection of smaller worlds

According to Robb Report, Olson Kundig designed this 6,500-square-foot Kona Coast residence as flat-roofed pavilions arranged around gardens and courtyards. The appeal is architectural rather than simply expansive: breaking the home into separate structures makes the spaces between buildings feel as important as the rooms themselves.
Views that unfold

Robb Report describes a nine-foot-tall slatted wood screen concealing the front door, followed by a view across the courtyard toward a cinder cone and the ocean beyond. That sequence is the compelling idea here: the landscape becomes a gradual reveal, rather than a single panorama delivered at the threshold.
Privacy with an outdoor connection

The primary suite occupies its own building, linked to the main house by a covered walkway, the publication reports. Each bedroom also opens onto a private courtyard with an outdoor shower. To us, those individual outdoor spaces are a particularly thoughtful counterpoint to the shared gathering areas.
Materials in conversation with the site

Robb Report identifies concrete walls, wood ceilings, cedar screens and basalt stone floors, with deep roof overhangs providing shade. Our favorite aspect is the restrained material vocabulary: it offers a way to read the architecture alongside the lava landscape without treating that rugged setting as mere scenery.

item.summary: The late music mogul's two-tiered aerie at The Ritz Tower in Manhattan's Midtown East neighborhood is now available for the first time.

illustrationDraft.title: We Love This Listing: A Park Avenue Penthouse Composed for Company
illustrationDraft.deck: Clive Davis’s Ritz Tower duplex pairs a nearly 48-foot great room with a screening room and a distinctly two-level approach to entertaining, according to Robb Report.
paragraphs: Two Apartments, One Ambitious Home

Robb Report traces the penthouse’s creation to Davis’s purchase of a full-floor apartment in 1985 and the unit below in 1989, followed by a collaboration with designers Vicente Wolf and Robert Metzger. Our take: the combination gives this home a more interesting premise than size alone.
A Great Room with a Musical Past

According to the publication, a private elevator landing opens onto the upper-level great room, where Davis kept his Steinway grand piano and hosted gatherings. At nearly 48 feet long, the room suggests an unusually generous setting for conversation and performance—not merely a place to arrange sofas.
A Different Register Downstairs

Robb Report places a formal dining room, a 12-seat Art Deco-style screening room and a larger secondary kitchen on the lower level, which has its own entrance. Editorially, that separation is the compelling move: dinner and a film have their own territory within the duplex.
Materials That Hold the Composition Together

The publication describes white oak herringbone-patterned floors alongside Macassar ebony paneling, cabinetry and bookcases. We love the contrast on paper: patterned oak and dark wood offer a decorative counterpoint to the home's expansive entertaining spaces, giving the feature a material story as well as a musical one.

item.summary: The Washington Park home features a stone arch the sellers won in a bidding war against Cher.

illustrationDraft.title: We Love This Listing: A Seattle Tudor With a Collector’s Point of View
illustrationDraft.deck: A 1924 home in Washington Park pairs substantial proportions with European finds and an unusually rich palette of woodwork, according to Robb Report.
paragraphs: Scale with a historical anchor

Robb Report identifies the gated Tudor at 530 36th Avenue E as a five-bedroom, seven-bathroom residence spanning 7,910 square feet. Those are mansion-sized numbers, but the more compelling editorial thread is how a century-old architectural framework accommodates a distinctly personal collection.
A renovation built around discoveries

According to the publication, owners Jonathan and Elizabeth Roberts undertook a major remodeling between 2000 and 2004, incorporating pieces sourced across Europe. A stone archway from Ireland found its place in the gardens. To us, that intersection of architecture and collecting is the feature’s strongest idea: renovation as composition rather than wholesale replacement.
Woodwork supplies the continuity

The report describes hand-waxed woodwork in the main living areas, pecan floorboards in the dining room and a cherry-paneled office. Read together, those material choices suggest a useful counterpoint to the collected antiques—a shared vocabulary of timber rather than a succession of unrelated showpieces.
The landscape gets a final word

Robb Report also notes a half-moon bench overlooking the water, with the Cascades beyond, and a landscaped rooftop deck offering a broader view. The appeal is the contrast: rooms organized around crafted surfaces, followed by outdoor spaces whose principal subject is the landscape.

paragraphs: Two waterfront connections

According to Robb Report, this four-story home in Barefoot Beach occupies roughly half an acre, with 120 feet of direct beachfront. The property also includes a canal-front boat slip and lift. For us, that combination is the waterfront story: the beach and boating each have a distinct place in the property’s design.
Art along the way

Robb Report describes a two-bedroom guest wing connected to the main house by an art gallery, with its own kitchen, living room and elevator. The appeal is architectural as much as decorative: a gallery turns the connection between shared and separate quarters into a space with a purpose of its own.
A top-floor departure

The publication places a 36-foot lap pool and spa on the top floor overlooking the Gulf, alongside a cabana and outdoor kitchen. That top-floor arrangement is the feature we find most distinctive. It gives swimming and outdoor entertaining an elevated setting rather than treating the pool as an automatic ground-level fixture.
Beyond the showpieces

Robb Report also details 103 support pilings, extensive waterproofing and drainage systems, and a whole-house backup generator. These reported specifications are not proof of storm-proof performance. They do, however, add a practical counterpoint to the gallery and pool—the less theatrical side of an unusually ambitious coastal home.
